newsitem.title: CHINA: China's faces new era after leader Deng dies.
newsitem.headline: China's faces new era after leader Deng dies.

text.p: China on Thursday began official mourning for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping as 1.2 billion people stepped into a new era without the political patriarch who masterminded the transformation of their nation.

Beijing's communist authorities voiced profound grief at the death late on Wednesday of the 92-year-old revolutionary who in the last 18 years of an extraordinary life turned China from a backward Stalinist nation to an emerging economic powerhouse.

The Communist Party, State Council and Central Military Commission awarded Deng five "greats", calling him "a great Marxist, a great proletarian revolutionary, statesman, military strategist and diplomat".

That was three more greats than had graced official eulogies to the late Chairman Mao Zedong, who died amidst an outpouring of national grief in 1976. His political legacy was largely unravelled under reform policies launched by practical-minded Deng in 1978.
The reaction of ordinary Chinese to Deng's passing was less uniformly effusive, ranging from shock and sadness to cold indifference.
"I feel a great sadness," said snack vendor Xie Weicai as he prepared his pavement stove for the morning's business, but his regret was not universal among the capital's residents.
"I would consider losing 100 yuan ($12) much sadder than the death of Deng Xiaoping," said one taxi driver on an early morning shift. "It has nothing to do with me."
Although Deng attracted much opprobrium in 1989 when he crushed pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, tributes poured in from around the world.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said he was saddened, calling Deng an "extraordinary figure on the world stage over the past two decades".
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien also voiced regret but said his feelings were mixed due to Deng's record on human rights.
Deng died almost within sight of Tiananmen Square, where troops and tanks of the People's Liberation Army, acting on his orders, killed hundreds of youthful activists.
China's official obituary for Deng praised his decision to crack down on the 1989 protests, a warning to people not to repeat those ill-fated demonstrations for more democracy.

"Amid domestic and international political disturbances in late 1980s and early 1990s, the Party and government, with the staunch and powerful support from comrade Deng Xiaoping and other veterans...maintained a clear-cut stand," it said.
The Foreign Ministry announced six days of mourning, indicating his funeral could take place on February 25.
Foreign dignitaries were not invited and foreign journalists were told they could not cover the event -- standard practice for the no-frills, non-state funeral requested by Deng.
Stock markets in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan -- which had widely been expected to slump when Deng died -- moved higher on Thursday after gyrating wildly at the opening.
"Investors feel that the last detectable uncertainty in China has been removed with the death of Deng Xiaoping," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities.
Deng, whose career spanned much of the 20th century, swept to power in 1978 after being purged three times and continued to weild great influence until well after he retired in 1990.
He led China from Mao Zedong's ultra-leftist fervour to a nation at its most stable and prosperous for nearly 200 years, and his influence reigned supreme until his death.
His economic reforms created in Southern China the biggest economic boom on earth.

The life-long nationalist died without achieving at least one dream -- to be present in Hong Kong when the colony, wrested from China by Britain in opium wars 150 years ago, returns to Beijing's sovereignty at midnight on June 30.
In Hong Kong, people took his death in their stride, saying it would hardly affect them.

The presidential office of Taiwan, which Deng also tried to woo with promises that China could accept both communist and capitalist systems, sent its condolences and urged a "peaceful, cooperative, prosperous new era" between Taipei and Beijing.
But the island, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, maintained a military alert.
